The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Looking at this problem, I need to understand what happens when Mark repeatedly replaces pairs $(a,b)$ with $(\gcd(a,b), \text{lcm}(a,b))$.

## Key Insight: Exponent Preservation

For each prime $p$, if $a$ has $p$-exponent $\alpha$ and $b$ has $p$-exponent $\beta$, then $\gcd(a,b)$ has $p$-exponent $\min(\alpha,\beta)$ and $\text{lcm}(a,b)$ has $p$-exponent $\max(\alpha,\beta)$. This means **the multiset of $p$-exponents across all numbers is preserved** for every prime $p$.

## Terminal Configuration

The process stops when no move changes the board, meaning for every pair, one number divides the other. The final numbers form a **chain under divisibility**: $c_1 \mid c_2 \mid \cdots \mid c_{2100}$.

Since the multiset of $p$-exponents is preserved and must be non-decreasing along the chain, the $p$-exponent of $c_i$ equals the **$i$-th smallest** value of $v_p(k)$ for $k \in \{1, \ldots, 2100\}$.

## Computing Exponents at Position 2026

For each prime $p$, the count of $k \in \{1,\ldots,2100\}$ with $v_p(k) = j$ is $\lfloor 2100/p^j \rfloor - \lfloor 2100/p^{j+1} \rfloor$.

| Prime | Ranges of positions | $v_p$ at position 2026 |
|-------|-------------------|----------------------|
| $2$ | $0$: 1–1050, $1$: 1051–1575, $2$: 1576–1838, $3$: 1839–1969, **$4$: 1970–2035** | **4** |
| $3$ | $0$: 1–1400, $1$: 1401–1867, $2$: 1868–2023, **$3$: 2024–2075** | **3** |
| $5$ | $0$: 1–1680, $1$: 1681–2016, **$2$: 2017–2084** | **2** |
| $7$ | $0$: 1–1800, **$1$: 1801–2058** | **1** |

For primes $p \geq 11$ with $p < 29$: position 2026 falls in the range where $v_p = 1$ (verified for $p = 11, 13, 17, 19, 23$).

For $p = 29$: only 72 numbers have $v_{29} \geq 1$, so 2028 numbers have $v_{29} = 0$. Since $2026 < 2028$, we get $v_{29} = 0$. All larger primes also give exponent 0.

## The 2026th Number

$$c_{2026} = 2^4 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 7^1 \cdot 11^1 \cdot 13^1 \cdot 17^1 \cdot 19^1 \cdot 23^1$$

## Counting Divisors

$$\tau(c_{2026}) = (4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^5 = 5 \times 4 \times 3 \times 32 = 1920$$

$$\boxed{1920}$$
